## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Uragajātaka* (Ja 154), translated as *The Snake*, is a birth story belonging to the Jātaka collection of the Khuddaka Nikāya [Catalog; SuttaCentral]. According to the narrative framework recorded in the tradition, the Buddha recounted this discourse while residing at Jetavana to address a quarrel among soldiers, opening with the phrase "Concealed within a stone" [SuttaCentral]. In secondary scholarship, Cecil Bendall cites Jātaka No. 154 in his edition of Śāntideva's *Śikṣāsamuccaya* as an instance demonstrating that serpents in Buddhist narrative literature are credited with the capacity for metamorphosis [Bendall 1902]. This text must be distinguished from the homonymous and widely known *Uragajātaka* of the *Pañcakanipāta* (Ja 354), which treats grief over a son's fatal snakebite [Bendall 1902; SuttaCentral].
Textual alignment data from DharmaNexus identifies no cross-language matches with Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan corpora at or above the threshold score of 10 [DharmaNexus]. Within Pali literature, DharmaNexus records ten matching passages totaling 765 characters of canonical and prose overlap with the second volume of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Dutiyo bhāgo), the longest continuous parallel spanning segments 1.4–2.4 of the text against segments 71–74 of the commentary [DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral registers four modern translations in four languages [SuttaCentral].
